Kedesh in Galilee in mount Naphtali, Shechem in mount Ephraim, and Kirjath-arba which is Hebron: the places of refuge the Lord gave us, and the roads to them are where the priests lay in wait.
precepts.point: There is the whoredom of Ephraim, Israel is defiled, and also, O Judah. It is not just Ephraim. Judah today is evil as hell; we are all off in many different ways.

precepts.text: And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron. The Lord shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust. That is what it looks like when the rain does not come.
precepts.point: When we harvest crops we look forward to the rain coming. We needed the rain to come. When it did not rain, we knew the Lord was not dealing with us. That is how he punished us. We read that in Deuteronomy 28. So the blessing the Lord will give us will be in the application of his laws.

note.label: God's People Need Charity, Healing & Trust

precepts.why:
Hosea ends with a promise: “he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth.” What is the analogy of the former and latter rain? It's going to be a blessing. When we harvested crops, we looked forward to the rain coming. We needed the rain to come. When it didn't rain, we knew the Lord wasn't dealing with us. That's how he punished us.

We read that in Deuteronomy 28: “And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron. The Lord shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust: from heaven shall it come down upon thee, until thou be destroyed.” That is what it looks like when the rain does not come: the heaven shut like brass, the ground hard as iron, and powder and dust in place of rain.

So when Hosea says the Lord will come unto us as the rain, it is the curse being lifted. “Come, and let us return unto the Lord: for he hath torn, and he will heal us”. We were torn by captivity and slavery, and he will heal us, meaning redeem us out of this situation. After two days, two thousand years, he revives us, and in the third day he raises us up to who we are, to our identity.

“Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the Lord”: if we follow on to apply what God tells us to do, then shall we be bound up and healed. The rain the Lord withheld in the curses comes back as a blessing, and that blessing will be in the application of his laws.

precepts.text: The verse Christ told the Pharisees to go and learn: he desires mercy and not sacrifice.
precepts.point: The Pharisees asked why Christ ate with publicans and sinners, the same spirit as the Pharisee in Luke 18. They that be whole need not a physician: the law is not made for the righteous but for the sick, the lawless and whoremongers. I will have mercy and not sacrifice, from Hosea, and I am come to call sinners to repentance.

note.label: The Mercy and Humility of King Manasseh

precepts.why:
When the Pharisees asked why Christ ate with publicans and sinners, he told them, “But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.” He was quoting Hosea: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”

God doesn’t care about sacrifice the way the Pharisees did. He cares about mercy. He desires mercy, and the knowledge of God, more than burnt offerings.

That is why Manasseh could be saved. Under the law there was no animal he could sacrifice to cover what he had done; he was finished. But the Lord desired mercy and not sacrifice, and so Manasseh could pray, “in me thou wilt shew all thy goodness: for thou wilt save me, that am unworthy, according to thy great mercy.”

precepts.text: I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings: the Lord said away with it through the prophets themselves.
precepts.point: Whosoever shall keep the whole law and yet offend in one point is guilty of all: the Christian says you cannot keep them, but the context is the royal law, as the next verse shows, he that said do not commit adultery said also do not kill. Speak and do as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty, since Christ redeemed us from the death the moral law carried; he shall have judgment without mercy that hath showed no mercy.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.why:
“Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth.” The word of God can slay; it is the spirit. “And thy judgments are as the light that goeth forth.”

“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” He was not about the sacrifice. That was a schoolmaster, a placeholder. He desired mercy and the knowledge of God.

The Lord eventually said away with it, through the prophets themselves. And that is where James 2:13 lands: “For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.” You shall receive no mercy if you show no mercy. Mercy rejoices against judgment: the Most High chooses to have mercy rather than to judge you for violating the royal law, and he looks for that same mercy in us toward our neighbour.

precepts.text: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
precepts.point: Jeremiah carries the same word: I spake not unto your fathers concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices, but this thing commanded I them, obey my voice. Yet they hearkened not, but walked in the counsels of their evil heart and went backward and not forward; speak all these words unto them, but they will not hearken. That is seen every sabbath on the streets.

note.label: Leviticus 6: The Trespass Offering and the Fire That Shall Never Go Out

precepts.why:
This is the scripture Christ was quoting: “I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”

The burnt offering burning all night on the altar was commanded, but the Most High desired the knowledge of God and obedience more than the burnt offerings. Israel put the sacrifices first and the commandments second, and it left them unable to know Christ when he stood in front of them.

precepts.text: He hath torn, and he will heal us; after two days will he revive us, and in the third day raise us up.
precepts.point: A thousand years is as a day to the Lord, and a day as a thousand years; as Hosea says, after two days He will revive us, and in the third day He will raise us up. The full teaching of that timing belongs to another class.

note.label: Numbers 24: A Star out of Jacob and the Latter Days

He hath torn, and He will heal us; after two days He will revive us, and in the third day raise us up. The full teaching of that timing belongs to another class.

precepts.text: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. This is what Christ was quoting, for the New Testament was not yet written; the knowledge of God is the keeping of the commandments.
precepts.point: Sacrifice was never the most important thing to the Lord; not the blood of bulls and of goats, but mercy upon one another and the keeping of the commandments. The sacrifices were added because of transgression, the animal's blood taken in your place so the Most High would not have to kill you; you read of it from Genesis 3, where the Lord took the skins after Adam sinned. Yet there were some things you could not sacrifice for, abominations for which a man's own blood was required.

precepts.point: Call upon the Most High in the day of trouble and he will deliver thee and thou shalt glorify him.

note.label: Psalm 50: The Mighty God Judges His People and the Wicked

precepts.why:
“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” This is the scripture Christ sent them to go and learn. The Most High testifies to Israel, “I am God, even thy God”, and says he will not reprove them for their sacrifices or burnt offerings; “If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof.” He never wanted the flesh of bulls or the blood of goats for their own sake. He wanted mercy and the knowledge of God.

So the offering he asks for is thanksgiving and paid vows, and to call upon him in the day of trouble. That is the mercy Hosea speaks of and the New Testament carries.

precepts.text: The Most High desired mercy and not sacrifice.
precepts.point: Christ did only what the Most High intended, to make His soul an offering for sin. The scripture always shows that sacrifice was temporary and that obedience and mercy were desired above it.

note.label: Acts 6: The Grecians Were Greek-Speaking Israelites

precepts.why:
“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” The Most High desired mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. The scripture always shows that sacrifice was temporary and that obedience and mercy were desired above it.

So the false witnesses were wrong. Christ did not change the customs Moses delivered; the only thing set aside was the sacrifice and offerings, and Hosea shows that was the Most High's desire all along.

note.label: Sabbath Morning Class: Messengers Of The Nation

precepts.why: Vesey could have went to Africa, but he stayed. It shows you his character: just like Moses. “By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season”. And look at that, brothers: “for a season”. It’s only gonna last for a season.

note.label: Sabbath Morning Class: Messengers Of The Nation

precepts.why:
“Then shall the righteous man stand in great boldness before the face of such as have afflicted him”. That’s how they describe Denmark Vesey. When you read this book it describes Nat Turner, it describes Gabriel Prosser: these men stood up in great boldness. That was during their time, the 1800s, and the Most High was using them.

Go a couple years ahead, to Marcus Garvey. Jamaica rejected him; he went to Panama, and everywhere he traveled the Negro was always at the bottom. When he came to America, Judah accepted Garvey’s teachings and gave him support: a significant following of ordinary working people, over one million followers in the 1920s and 30s. Before 1865 Denmark Vesey was recruiting slaves, persistent, setting up men under him that had different talents; almost a hundred years later Garvey was recruiting, recruiting, recruiting, because they saw the same thing Denmark saw, the same thing Gabriel Prosser saw, the same thing Nat Turner saw: you have to liberate your people.

Malcolm X’s parents, Earl and Louise Little, were the typical Garvey family. Wherever they went they started chapters; they were always mobile, but always teaching, recruiting people to join the movement. And mind you, they didn’t even have the truth, but they understood how our people are oppressed, at the bottom. Louise Little was the secretary of the Lansing UNIA and wrote the reports of meetings; Garvey set up the Black Cross Nurses, women who went to the homes of Garvey families to make sure they were healthy and getting enough food. These sisters was getting down. There’s always stuff to do for the woman. All you got to do is get in where you fit in: you know your talents, you know how you can assist. Everybody don’t have the same talent, everybody don’t have the same gift. That sister didn’t have the truth, but she understood to assist and support black men. They were not leaders, not heads of the organization, but they were local and they were committed. That’s the point: that you are committed.

Gil Noble says his parents taught him not to confront racism but to get around it, to accommodate, because they didn’t want him to get killed or join one of these groups. That’s the same way I grew up; I rarely heard racism dealt with. Some of your parents raised you to be timid, to assimilate; some raised you to be an agitator. We’re all coming with different personalities, different spirits, but the Most High is calling us to this truth. Garvey was in the streets of Harlem, teaching on the street about pride, standing up for your race. It’s the same thing we’re doing now. The only difference, brothers: this movement is God’s movement. All the movements before were movements of men. They did whatever they could for their people, being used by the Most High, but it was not the Most High’s movement, because they only understood so much. You got to have respect: with the little that they knew, Nat Turner and Denmark Vesey still did a lot for their people.

note.label: The Getaway 3

precepts.why: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice”: and who brought that mercy? Christ. “And the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings”: what’s the knowledge? The laws of God; a brother answered Malachi 2:7, the priest’s lips shall keep knowledge. So the Most High desired the law more than burnt offerings, showing he was going to get rid of that; it was temporary, to train us up into accepting his son.

note.label: The Song Of Moses & The Song Of The Lamb

precepts.why:
He said in three days. “Come, and let us return unto the Lord: for he hath torn”: he tore us in captivity, “and he will heal us”: he will revive us. “He hath smitten, and he will bind us up”: he’s going to bind us back to 12 tribes again.

Watch this: “After two days will he revive us”. If two days are past, what day would it be? The third. So we’re being revived. “In the third day”: that’s the day we’re living in right now, “he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.” That is the rising of the dead men of Isaiah 26:19, together with his dead body.

note.label: Bishop Nathanyel | Revelation 1 A Visit From The Lord

precepts.why:
Something about that thousand-year period. “Come, and let us return unto the Lord:” So the prophet Hosea says come, let us return unto the Lord. “for he hath torn, and he will heal us;” Meaning he put us in slavery and he's going to bring us out. “he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.” Same thing.

“After two days will he revive us:” Y'all see that right there? That two days is 2,000 years. It is literally saying after 2,000 years will he revive us. What we see here right now, that's online right before us, this is us being revived. Notice the word after: after two days. So if two days has passed, what day is it? The third day. “in the third day he will raise us up,” We're in that third day. We haven't been raised up yet, but we're being revived. The reviving is us waking up to the truth; the raising us up is to the stature we are meant to be, when we rule this world. “and we shall live in his sight.” He didn't tell us what part of the third day he's going to raise us, though we know we're in it because we're being revived. So we're just waiting.

That's a heavy mystery right there. The average will read day and go, two days. Remember 2,000 years ago what happened: Christ died on the cross, was resurrected and ascended upon high. That is why Revelation 1:1 says things which must shortly come to pass.

note.label: Sons of Jacob: A Shadow of Things to Come

precepts.why:
We read Hosea 5:15, that he left and returned to his place. But right after that, once we repent: “Come, and let us return unto the Lord.” He returned to his place, so now we have to go after him and seek him, because we backslid, moonwalking away from the Most High God.

“For he hath torn, and he will heal us.” He tore us apart in slavery. The yokes of iron came off, but we were bugged out of our minds with religion, doctrine, philosophy and the ideology of men. “He hath smitten, and he will bind us up.” He has already started that process. That is why we are here getting our minds right, why we no longer call ourselves Jamaicans, Haitians or American blacks, why we no longer carry the last names Robinson, Patterson or Jean-Claude. We surnamed ourselves Israel, because that is what the Bible says, and we know who we are now.

That is the Father in the midst of Israel.

note.label: Zechariah's Leadership

precepts.why: “Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the Lord”. “His going forth is prepared as the morning”: as the morning. “And he shall come unto us as the rain”: that’s that Holy Spirit raining down on us, “as the latter and former rain unto the earth”, like the end gathering seasons, the harvest and the ingathering. That’s the rain asked of the Lord in the time of the latter rain.

note.label: Awake and Return: Overcoming Babylon's Hypnosis

points: “Come, and let us return unto the Lord: for he hath torn, and he will heal us”. He hath torn, but will heal us. In the healing process he used many different figures to start to heal us, and here is an example: Denmark Vesey, from the book Before the Mayflower by Lerone Bennett Jr. Vesey tried to have a successful slave insurrection, but it was told to the slave masters and they hung him. Look at where his frame of mind was during that time for his people.

Vesey won a lottery and purchased his freedom. He worked as a carpenter in Charleston, South Carolina, accumulated money and property, and was respected by Negroes and whites; by his own admission he was satisfied with his own condition. Yet he risked everything in a bold effort to free other men. He had the chance to go to Liberia, to Africa, and he decided to stay; he wanted to stay and see what he could do for his fellow creatures. Denmark Vesey was from St. Thomas, and they brought him to America; he was some twenty years the slave of a slave trader, traveled widely, learned several languages, and learned that slavery was evil. He had a deep and unquenchable hatred of slavery and slaveholders, and reached a point where he could not bear to have a white person in his presence.

For four or five years he played the role of an agitator. Men, he saw, must not only be dissatisfied; they must be so dissatisfied they will act. You can’t just be upset; you have to be so angry you will commit action. What is the action that we’re doing? Organizing, teaching. But we can’t be like our people: you get mad and you burn down a neighborhood. No, no. We get mad, but we organize.

He told the slaves their lives were so miserable that even death would be an improvement. He read to them from the Bible how the children of Israel were delivered out of Egypt from bondage, but warned that God helps those who help themselves, and always the words of Joshua were on his lips. If he saw slaves with the white men in the street he would rebuke them, and when they replied, but we are slaves, he would say with biting sarcasm, you deserve to be slaves. This brother was cold. He was from St. Thomas, so you know what tribe that is. Asked what can we do, he would tell the story of Hercules and the wagoner whose wagon was stuck at the bottom of the hill: the wagoner began to cry and pray, and Hercules told him to put the whip to the team. Always, everywhere, Denmark Vesey was teaching. He said, we are free, but the white people here won’t let us be so, and the only way is to raise up and fight the whites. Vesey was all about helping his people.

He employed every stratagem to induce them to join him. It wasn’t a one-time thing; it was constant, persistent effort. Vesey was free, and he would remain with slaves and teach slaves, reading them every passage in the newspapers that related to St. Domingo, Haiti, and every pamphlet he could lay his hands on that had any connection with slavery. Ridiculing, taunting, threatening, he gained a hold on the minds of the Negroes in Charleston; many slaves feared him more than they feared their masters, and one man said he feared Vesey more than he feared God. He didn’t play.

Then Vesey switched from the role of agitator to the role of organizer. Around Christmas of 1821 he chose lieutenants and perfected his organization. This isn’t a one-man job when it comes to waking our people up; it is collective effort. He enlisted slave artisans and class leaders in the Methodist church. He had Gullah Jack, an African-born sorcerer who practiced voodoo, and blind Philip, who reportedly could see ghosts: timid recruits were carried to his house, and blind Philip would ask them why they looked so timorous and quote Holy Scripture, ‘let not your heart be troubled’. The chief lieutenant was Peter, a first-rate ship carpenter with an organizing ability bordering on genius; ice water ran in his veins. He volunteered for the most difficult assignment, the surprise and capture of the main guardhouse.

Peter was in charge of organization; he decided who should be approached and who shouldn’t. He pinpointed the greatest danger to a slave revolt, the house servants: don’t mention it to those waiting men who receive presents of old coats from their masters, or they’ll betray us. So Peter said, you let me deal with the Coons. Vesey and Peter perfected a cell-like organization: only the leaders knew the details, and the average recruit knew nothing except the name of his leader, so a single recruit arrested could not endanger the whole plot. Whole plantations signed up and weapons were constructed. It has been estimated that some nine thousand slaves were recruited. The reason Vesey wasn’t able to carry out his mission is because too many people knew about it, and eventually brothers sold out.
